chunk_findings.detail: The clamp fixes the reported direction (a trailing `]` after the id's closing `]` made depth negative and swallowed the following separator) but trades it for the opposite failure for any single node id whose param value contains two `]` and then a comma inside the id's brackets. `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]")` — the node id for `@pytest.mark.parametrize("s", ["a]b]c,d"])` — traces as: `[`→1, `]`→0, second `]`→`max(0,-1)=0`, then `,` is seen at depth 0 and splits, returning `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c", "d]"]`. Under the old code the second `]` drove depth to -1, so the `,` was kept and the function returned the single entry `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]"]` — which is the correct parse (the comma is inside the id's brackets). The clamped version therefore rejects a regression test that actually exists: `_unresolved_tests` will check `tests/a.py::test[a]b]c` and `d]`, find neither, and report the valid node id as missing. This is the mirror image of the bug being fixed, so the `max(0, ...)` heuristic is only sound when the deeper `]` is the id's final character; it needs the same treatment its sibling `_looks_like_several` gets or a bracket-count that is not reset by an in-value `]`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py `_split_outside_brackets` (the `depth = max(0, ...)` line)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic decides a `]` closes the parametrize id's brackets whenever the next character is `""`, `,`, `;` or whitespace. But the whole reason for this bug is that a parametrize value may itself contain `]`, and such a value may also contain `,`/`;` (the sibling test `tests/a.py::t[1,2;3]` already asserts commas/semicolons inside brackets must not split). When the embedded `]` is immediately followed by a separator, the code wrongly treats it as the closing bracket.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b]")`. Tracing line 86-88: at `[`, `inside=True`; the `a` is appended; at the first `]`, `spec[i+1]` is `','`, so `after in ",;"` is true and `inside` is set to `False`; the following `,` then hits `if ch in ",;" and not inside` and splits. The call returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]']` (and the two-entry list `"tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/b.py::u"` returns three entries `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]', 'tests/b.py::u']`) instead of the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b]`. This is structurally identical to the case the new test covers (`tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]`, where the embedded `]` happens to be followed by `b` rather than the comma): one `[`, two `]`, comma between them; the outcome flips purely on the character after the first `]`, so `t[a],b]` is split inside its own brackets while `t[a]b]c,d]` is not. A value like `t[a] b,c]` (embedded `]` followed by whitespace then a comma) fails the same way via `after.isspace()`. The result is a spurious extra entry (e.g. `b]`) that `_unresolved_tests` will see as a missing test, i.e. the same "missing test never resolved / wrong resolution" failure mode this change was meant to eliminate.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:86-88 (`_split_outside_brackets`)

chunk_findings.detail: Over-split: any bracketed parametrize value containing a comma followed by a token ending in `.py` is torn apart, even though the comma is inside the id's brackets. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]")`: after `[` `bracketed=True`, every `,`/`;` is tested against `_NEXT_PATH.match(spec, i+1)`; at the comma the remainder is `b.py]`, which the regex matches (`[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` matches `.py`, `(?![\w.])` sees `]`), so it splits. The function returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b.py]']` instead of the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]']`. This is exactly the case the new test `test_a_value_whose_inner_bracket_meets_a_separator_stays_one_entry` covers for `t[a],b]` — it only passes because `b]` lacks the `.py`; the sibling input `t[a.py,b.py]` fails the same way (returns `['tests/a.py::t[a.py', 'b.py]']`). The pre-change code (comma suppressed while `inside`) returned one entry here, so this is a regression introduced by the diff, and the new tests do not exercise a value token ending in `.py`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets (`_NEXT_PATH` + `bracketed` condition)

chunk_findings.detail: Under-split: once an entry is bracketed, a following separator is ignored unless the next entry starts with a file path, so a legitimate non-path entry is merged. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x")`: at the comma `bracketed=True` and the remainder ` pytest -k x` contains no `.py`, so no split; the result is the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x']`. The function's own contract ("entries separated by ',' or ';'") and the newly added `test_entries_without_brackets_split_as_before` treat `pytest -k x` as a separate entry (it splits there only because no `[` preceded it), so the behavior is inconsistent and the command is swallowed into the node id, which is the same failure mode (an entry that is never seen as its own item) that this change set out to fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets (`_NEXT_PATH` + `bracketed` condition)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_closes_unopened` scans the *entire* remainder `spec[i+1:]`, which includes the following entries, so an unbalanced `]` inside the *second* entry's parametrize value is misread as "closing a bracket the current entry never opened", and the split is suppressed.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]")`.

- At the comma, `cur == "tests/a.py::t[x]"` ends with `]` (first condition passes).
- `rest == "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"`. Walking it: `[` → depth 1, the first `]` → depth 0, then the trailing `]` → depth −1, so `_closes_unopened` returns `True`.
- The `and not _closes_unopened(...)` term is therefore `False`, the separator is appended to `cur`, and the function returns the single entry `["tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]` instead of the two entries `["tests/a.py::t[x]", "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]`.

The docstring itself declares `t[x]y]` a legitimate parametrize id, so `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is a valid second entry (its value is `a]b`). Because the list is not split, `_unresolved_tests` only looks at `tests/a.py::t` and the genuinely missing `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is never flagged — precisely the failure mode Bfc9daca269 is supposed to close, still reachable whenever the second bracketed entry's value contains a `]`. The added test only covers a second entry with balanced brackets (`tests/c.py::d[e]`), so it does not exercise this case.

Note this is a regression relative to the removed `_NEXT_PATH` approach, which matched the second entry by its leading `… .py` token and split correctly here.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py (_split_outside_brackets / _closes_unopened)

chunk_findings.detail:
Input: `tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]`.

This is a single node id whose value is `a],b.py,c` (the documented shape `t[a],b]` generalised, i.e. the separator before `]` is inside the id, and the rest `b.py,c]` closes a `]` it never opened). On the *old* code the first comma sees `cur == "tests/x.py::t[a]"` (ends with `]`), and `_closes_unopened("b.py,c]")` is `True`, so the branch is not taken and the spec is correctly kept as one entry.

On the *new* code `_NEXT_PATH.match("b.py,c]", 0)` succeeds: `[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` consumes `.py`, and the lookahead `(?=::|[\s,;]|$)` matches the following `,`. So the entry is split at the first comma, `bracketed` is reset to `False`, and the remaining comma (now "outside brackets") splits again. The function returns three entries:

    ["tests/x.py::t[a]", "b.py", "c]"]   # after
    ["tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]"]         # before (correct)

`b.py` here is a fragment of the parametrize value, not a following test path, so `_unresolved_tests` now resolves bogus entries (`b.py`, `c]`) instead of the real one. The asymmetry is visible in the regex's own comment: `t[a],b.py]` is handled (the `]` is not in the lookahead set), but `t[a],b.py,c]` / `t[a],b.py::c]` are not — the new "a test path follows" reason overrides `_closes_unopened` even when the following `.py` token is a value rather than an entry.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets (the `_NEXT_PATH.match(...) or ...` clause)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_malformed` encodes the assumption "a node id's parametrize part is its LAST part", so it flags any entry that contains `[` but does not end in `]`. Pytest node ids violate this for class-level parametrization: a class decorated with `pytest.mark.parametrize` produces ids of the form `tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m` (the parametrize bracket sits on the class, followed by `::method`), so such an id is a *valid, well-formed* node id but `_malformed` returns `True` for it. This makes the global minimum prefer merging a list that should split. Concretely, for

    spec = "tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"

the only separator is the comma. Cutting there gives entries `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m"` (flagged malformed → 1) and `"tests/b.py::test_n[y]"` (valid → 0), i.e. `(1, -2, …)`. Not cutting gives the single entry `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"`, which ends in `]` with `[` before it, so it is *not* flagged, i.e. `(0, -1, …)`. The `min` picks the fewer-malformed single entry, so `_split_outside_brackets` returns one entry even though there are two perfectly well-formed readings — directly violating the design's own rule that a genuinely ambiguous, well-formed input must resolve to *more* entries. The second test is then never checked on its own, which is the same failure mode the change was supposed to fix for `'tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'`; it just moves the trigger to any list whose first element is a class-parametrized node id and whose second element ends in `]`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py: `_malformed` / `_split_outside_brackets`

chunk_findings.detail: The new first clause exempts *any* piece that contains whitespace and doesn't itself start with a `....py::` path, which is broader than “a command”: a whitespace can also live inside a node id's parametrize value. Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[a],hello world]"` — a single valid node id for a string parameter whose id is `a],hello world` (pytest keeps spaces in string ids; `_split_outside_brackets` is documented to handle params holding `]`, `[`, `,`, `;`, and space is no different) — the whole entry ends in `]` so `_malformed(whole)` is False, and the cut at the comma yields pieces `tests/a.py::t[a]` (well formed) and `hello world]`, which is also reported not malformed precisely because of the new whitespace clause. Both readings therefore have zero malformed entries, and the tie-break documented in the changed docstring (“the one with more entries wins”) makes `_split_outside_brackets` return `["tests/a.py::t[a]", "hello world]"]` — it splits one existing test id into a truncated id plus the garbage fragment `hello world]`. Before this change the old `_malformed` flagged `hello world]` (`]` with no `[`) as malformed, so the whole string was kept as a single well-formed entry and the real node id was resolvable; the added whitespace exemption is what introduces the wrong split, so a valid regression test is now reported unresolved (or a bogus `hello world]` test is looked up).

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug (Bfc9daca269) lives in `_split_outside_brackets`, and that function is never touched by this diff — the only production hunks are in `_unresolved_tests` and the new `_bare_names`/`_PARAMS`. So the probe from the intent still fails: `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')` sees depth 1 at `[`, back to 0 at the `]` after `x`, still 0 through `y`, then `]` drives it to −1; the following comma is at depth −1, not 0, so no split happens and the call still returns the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2']`. The new `_bare_names` does not compensate: for `names = 't[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'` the regex `\[.*?\](?=::|\s|$)` finds no `]` followed by `::`/whitespace/EOS, so it falls through to `bare.split('[', 1)[0]`, yielding `['t']` — `_unresolved_tests` still only verifies `tests/a.py::t` and never resolves `tests/missing.py::t2`, i.e. the invalid regression test is still accepted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py::_split_outside_brackets

chunk_findings.detail: The test that is supposed to guard the intent's fix cannot fail on the unfixed code. Its input `"tests/a.py::t[a],tests/b.py::u[x]]"` puts the comma at bracket depth 0: `[a]` opens and closes before the comma, so even the unclamped `depth += {'[':1,']':-1}` splitter still hits depth 0 at that comma and returns the two expected entries. The negative-depth condition the bug is about (a `]` inside the id *before* the comma, as in `t[x]y],...`) never occurs here — the extra `]` in `u[x]]` sits after the comma and can only affect a later comma, of which there is none. A regression test that actually fails on the unfixed code needs the comma met while depth is already negative, e.g. `"tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/b.py::u"`, which the added test does not do, so `ddflow complete ... --regression-test` would close the bug on a test that passes either way.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change does not fix the bug it is attached to. The intent says the defect is that `_split_outside_brackets` does `depth += {'[':1,']':-1}` without clamping, so a `]` inside a parametrize id drives depth negative and a following comma is never treated as a separator. But this diff modifies only `_bare_names`; `_split_outside_brackets` is untouched and its depth arithmetic still goes negative.

Concretely, with the exact probe input from the intent, after this change `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')` still returns the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2']` (the `]` after `y` puts depth at -1, so the comma is considered "inside brackets"). `_unresolved_tests` therefore still never receives `tests/missing.py::t2` as a separate entry, and a missing regression test is still accepted — the reported bug is unaddressed.

The new `_bare_names` filter cannot compensate. Applied to that glued entry it removes `[x]`, yielding parts `['tests/a.py', 'ty],tests/missing.py', 't2']`; the filter drops every part containing `]`, so the middle part is discarded and the result is `['tests/a.py', 't2']`. The `tests/missing.py` file path is gone entirely, so nothing downstream inspects it. Fixing `_bare_names` only suppresses a phantom *name*; it never restores the *split* the bug is about.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py::_bare_names (diff touches `_bare_names`, not `_split_outside_brackets`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change reworks `_bare_names`'s regexes but never touches the function the bug report names as the culprit: `_split_outside_brackets`, which still does `depth += {'[': 1, ']': -1}` with no `max(0, ...)` clamp (unlike its sibling `_looks_like_several`). Because the diff does not alter that splitter, the reported probe still produces the failing behavior: for `'tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'`, `[` raises `depth` to 1, the `]` in `t[x]` drops it back to 0, and the second `]` in `t[x]y]` drives it to -1. From then on no comma is seen at depth 0, so `_split_outside_brackets` yields ONE entry, `_bare_names` is only ever handed the `tests/a.py::t...` prefix, and `tests/missing.py::t2` is never checked — i.e. a nonexistent regression test is still accepted (exactly the accept-invalid bug Bfc9daca269 describes). The regression test added in this diff does not exercise that path: it feeds `_unresolved_tests` a single, comma-free id, `"tests/test_a.py::TestC[a] b]::test_m_missing"`, so it can pass green while the reported unbalanced-`]` / comma-splitting bug remains unfixed. Either `_split_outside_brackets` must be clamped (or replaced by a split that tracks the `]`-in-id case), or the change does not fix the stated bug.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug (Bfc9daca269) is that `_split_outside_brackets` updates depth with `{'[': 1, ']': -1}` without clamping, so a stray `]` in a parametrize id drives depth negative and a following top-level comma is no longer recognized as a separator. The probe in the intent, `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')`, must return two entries. This patch contains no edit to `_split_outside_brackets` (the only changed lines are the import list in `__init__.py` and a deletion in `tests/test_module_splits.py`). Running the probe against the code after this diff still returns the single unsplit string `['tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2']`, `_unresolved_tests` still inspects only `tests/a.py::t`, and `fixed`/`invalid` still accept a regression test that does not exist. The bug is not fixed; the imports added are the exported-test-surface names, not the fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py `_split_outside_brackets`

chunk_findings.detail: The patch deletes `assert set(homes) <= set(DEFINED[pkg.__name__])`, which was the guard that every function/class actually defined in the package's modules is also present in the module's `DEFINED` registry. After this deletion, a module that defines `def foo()` but omits `foo` from `DEFINED` passes the test silently — `homes` will simply not contain the entry that would violate the subset check, and the only remaining assertion is about *duplicate* homes, not about missing registrations. Concretely, if `foo` is later moved into a new module without being added to `DEFINED[pkg.__name__]`, the test that previously failed now passes, so the registry used by the split-detection code can silently drift out of sync with the code. That is a loss of coverage, not a fix for the bracket-depth bug.

If `ddflow.infra.git` does import `subprocess` — which is exactly what the header asserts, and which the old, passing `.importlinter` baseline must therefore have suppressed — then the joined config the guard test builds is missing that allowlist entry. Running import-linter against the joined config will then report `ddflow.infra.git -> subprocess` as a violation of the `subprocess-home` contract, so the guard that previously passed now fails (behaviour is not identical to the old `.importlinter`); conversely, if the header is wrong and git does not import subprocess, the file still contradicts itself. The missing home entry for the second named owner is the concrete divergence: header says two home modules, baseline provides one.

chunk_findings.detail: The rule (and this function's own docstring) says the second rung is *the nearest* directory below the test dir, and only if that misses does it fall to the file's name. The code instead emits one "directory alone" rung for **every** directory between the file and the nearest test directory: `rungs = [([name], dirs), *(([d], []) for d in dirs), ([name], [])]`. For a nested data file this changes the outcome. Take `tests/fixtures/mcp-schema/schema.json`: `_dirs_below_tests` returns `["mcp-schema", "fixtures"]` (nearest first). Suppose the test that actually reads it builds the sub-directory from a variable and spells only `"schema.json"` (the B20b7744905 case, name built at run time), and some other test spells the standalone token `fixtures` (e.g. it references `tests/fixtures/other/...`). Rung 1 misses (no `mcp-schema`/`fixtures` token in the reader). The code then tries `mcp-schema` (no hit) and then `fixtures`, hits the unrelated test on the very first token match, and `break`s — so it selects a test that never reads `schema.json` and never reaches the intended final rung `[name]`, which would have selected the real reader. Intended behavior (rung 2 = nearest dir only, then rung 3 = name) selects the reader. Since `fixtures` is spelled by almost any suite that has `tests/fixtures/...`, this over/under-selection triggers for every changed file nested more than one level under a test directory where no test names the immediate sub-directory.

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring promises the word is matched "not inside a longer name", but the lookbehind excludes `.` while the lookahead does not, so a bare name followed by a dotted suffix still matches. With `word = "schema.json"` the pattern is `(?<![\w.-])schema\.json(?![\w-])`; in the text `"fixtures/schema.json.orig"` the character after `schema.json` is `.`, which is not in `[\w-]`, so the negative lookahead succeeds and `_names` returns True. Consequently, when the changed data file is `tests/fixtures/schema.json`, a test that only reads the backup `tests/fixtures/schema.json.orig` is selected even though it cannot read the changed file, contradicting the stated "not inside a longer name" boundary (the mirror-image case `old_schema.json` is correctly rejected by the lookbehind, showing the asymmetry is unintentional).

chunk_findings.detail: The rung list builds a "directory alone" rung for *every* directory in `dirs`, not just the nearest one, contradicting the stated rule ("…; failing that, the nearest such directory; failing that, the file's name; stop at the first rung that hits") and the function's own docstring ("the nearest such directory alone"). Concretely, with tests living only under `tests/`, a change to `tests/fixtures/data/report.json` makes `_dirs_below_tests` return `["data", "fixtures"]`. If no test spells `data` but many tests spell `fixtures` (for their own, unrelated fixture files), rung 2 skips past the nearest directory, matches `fixtures`, and selects every such test — tests that never name `report.json` or its directory `data` and therefore cannot read the changed file. And because selection stops at the first hitting rung, a test that *does* read the file by its exact name (the intended last-resort name rung) is never reached. Under the stated rule the nearest directory failing should fall through to the file's name, not to a farther, generic ancestor directory.

chunk_findings.detail: The right-hand boundary is `(?![\w-])`, which omits `.`, while the left-hand boundary is `(?<![\w.-])`, which includes it. The helper therefore still matches a name as a prefix of a longer dotted name, contradicting its documented contract ("not inside a longer name"): `_names("tmp_path / 'LICENSE.txt'", "LICENSE")` returns True, as does `_names('"fixtures.json"', "fixtures")`. Given a changed data file `tests/fixtures/x.json` (whose nearest directory rung is `fixtures`), a test that only writes its own `fixtures.json` is selected as a reader of `x.json` even though it cannot read it. Excluding `.` on the right, as on the left, would remove these false positives.

But the rule it is testing keeps a third rung, "failing that, the file's name", which does exactly what the comment says is invalid. The added test only observes `test_licence_writer` being skipped because `test_conformance` (which does read a COPYING) hits rung 1 first, so "stop at the first rung" masks the bug; the bare-name rung is never actually exercised. Concretely, give the rule a changed file whose directory nothing spells: add/modify `tests/other/COPYING` (no test source mentions `other`). chunk_findings.detail:
The rung list drops the final `([name], [])` fallback whenever `dirs` is non-empty, so a file below a test directory is only ever matched by "name + some directory" or by the nearest directory alone. A test that reads the file by spelling only its name (the directory coming from an imported constant) is now missed, even though the old code selected it. Concrete input: `changed = ["tests/fixtures/schema.json"]`, `tests = ["tests/test_reader.py"]`, with no test file living under `tests/fixtures`, so `dirs == ["fixtures"]` and `name == "schema.json"`. The test source is

```python
from conftest import FIXTURES
def test_r():
    (FIXTURES / "schema.json").read_text()
```

with `FIXTURES = Path(__file__).parent / "fixtures"` defined in `tests/conftest.py`. The test text contains `schema.json` but not `fixtures`, so rung 1 (`name` + one of `dirs`) fails, rung 2 (`dirs[0] == "fixtures"`) fails, and there is no longer a bare-name rung; the test that does read the file is not selected. The removed rung was exactly the "last resort" for paths assembled at run time, and the stated rationale for dropping name-alone ("a bare `LICENSE` or `.gitattributes` is also in tests that write one of their own") only justifies it for generic names, not for a specific name like `schema.json`; the implementation applies it to every nested file, so the narrowing is broader than its justification and produces a real false negative.

chunk_findings.detail: The "failing that, the file's NEAREST directory alone" rung is built from the first element of `dirs`, but `dirs` holds the directories between the test root and the file in path order (outermost first), so `dirs[0]` is the *farthest* directory, not the nearest. For a changed file `tests/fixtures/guard_baselines/case.json` with tests under `tests/`, `dirs == ["fixtures", "guard_baselines"]`, so the second rung tests for the word `fixtures`. Consequence: (a) the test that actually reads the file and spells only its immediate directory (`guard_baselines`) is never matched, because it does not spell the generic `fixtures` — e.g. `os.path.join(BASE, "guard_baselines", name)` with `BASE` defined as `"fixtures"` elsewhere selects nothing, whereas `dirs[-1]` would match; and (b) conversely every test that merely names `fixtures` (i.e. reads any fixture at all) is selected as a reader of `case.json`, which is exactly the over-broad match the new docstring says the nearest-directory rung exists to avoid ("a farther directory (`fixtures`) is in every test that reads any fixture at all"). The code therefore contradicts both its own docstring ("NEAREST") and the retained comment ("most specific first"); the rung must use the deepest directory (`dirs[-1]`), not `dirs[0]`.

The code instead emits one "directory alone" rung for **every** directory between the file and the nearest test directory: `rungs = [([name], dirs), *(([d], []) for d in dirs), ([name], [])]`. For a nested data file this changes the outcome. Take `tests/fixtures/mcp-schema/schema.json`: `_dirs_below_tests` returns `["mcp-schema", "fixtures"]` (nearest first). Suppose the test that actually reads it builds the sub-directory from a variable and spells only `"schema.json"` (the B20b7744905 case, name built at run time), and some other test spells the standalone token `fixtures` (e.g. it references `tests/fixtures/other/...`). Rung 1 misses (no `mcp-schema`/`fixtures` token in the reader). The code then tries `mcp-schema` (no hit) and then `fixtures`, hits the unrelated test on the very first token match, and `break`s — so it selects a test that never reads `schema.json` and never reaches the intended final rung `[name]`, which would have selected the real reader. Intended behavior (rung 2 = nearest dir only, then rung 3 = name) selects the reader. Since `fixtures` is spelled by almost any suite that has `tests/fixtures/...`, this over/under-selection triggers for every changed file nested more than one level under a test directory where no test names the immediate sub-directory.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/testselect.py:_data_readers (the `rungs` list)

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring promises the word is matched "not inside a longer name", but the lookbehind excludes `.` while the lookahead does not, so a bare name followed by a dotted suffix still matches. With `word = "schema.json"` the pattern is `(?<![\w.-])schema\.json(?![\w-])`; in the text `"fixtures/schema.json.orig"` the character after `schema.json` is `.`, which is not in `[\w-]`, so the negative lookahead succeeds and `_names` returns True. Consequently, when the changed data file is `tests/fixtures/schema.json`, a test that only reads the backup `tests/fixtures/schema.json.orig` is selected even though it cannot read the changed file, contradicting the stated "not inside a longer name" boundary (the mirror-image case `old_schema.json` is correctly rejected by the lookbehind, showing the asymmetry is unintentional).

chunk_findings.detail:
The rung list drops the final `([name], [])` fallback whenever `dirs` is non-empty, so a file below a test directory is only ever matched by "name + some directory" or by the nearest directory alone. A test that reads the file by spelling only its name (the directory coming from an imported constant) is now missed, even though the old code selected it. Concrete input: `changed = ["tests/fixtures/schema.json"]`, `tests = ["tests/test_reader.py"]`, with no test file living under `tests/fixtures`, so `dirs == ["fixtures"]` and `name == "schema.json"`. The test source is

```python
from conftest import FIXTURES
def test_r():
    (FIXTURES / "schema.json").read_text()
```

with `FIXTURES = Path(__file__).parent / "fixtures"` defined in `tests/conftest.py`. The test text contains `schema.json` but not `fixtures`, so rung 1 (`name` + one of `dirs`) fails, rung 2 (`dirs[0] == "fixtures"`) fails, and there is no longer a bare-name rung; the test that does read the file is not selected. The removed rung was exactly the "last resort" for paths assembled at run time, and the stated rationale for dropping name-alone ("a bare `LICENSE` or `.gitattributes` is also in tests that write one of their own") only justifies it for generic names, not for a specific name like `schema.json`; the implementation applies it to every nested file, so the narrowing is broader than its justification and produces a real false negative.

chunk_findings.detail:
The name‑alone rung is documented as the "last resort" that catches a test which builds the path from a directory constant (`FIXTURES / "corpus.jsonl"`), but it is unreachable whenever the file's NEAREST directory name also occurs in any unrelated test, because the preceding rung (`([dirs[0]], [])`) short‑circuits the loop.

Concretely, take a changed data file directly below a fixture directory: `tests/fixtures/corpus.jsonl`. For it `dirs == ["fixtures"]`, so the rungs are `(["corpus.jsonl"], ["fixtures"])`, `(["fixtures"], [])`, `(["corpus.jsonl"], [])`. Let the true reader be a test whose source contains `FIXTURES / "corpus.jsonl"` where `FIXTURES` is an imported constant; matching is case‑sensitive, so this test does not contain the lowercase token `fixtures` and therefore misses rung 1 (needs `corpus.jsonl` *and* a dir) and would only be caught by rung 3. But the change's own docstring states "`fixtures` is in every test that reads any fixture at all", so some other test (e.g. one containing `fixtures/other.txt`) matches rung 2; rung 2 is non‑empty, the loop records those hits and `break`s before evaluating rung 3, and the constant‑building reader is never selected.

So the input `tests/fixtures/corpus.jsonl` + reader `FIXTURES / "corpus.jsonl"` + any other test mentioning `fixtures` misses a test that does read the file — i.e. the newly added name‑alone rung fails to do the one thing it was added for in exactly the example given in the docstring. The same preemption happens for rung 1: if any test spells the file name together with the lowercased directory, the loop stops there and the constant reader is still missed.

chunk_findings.detail: The new last-resort rule ("else the file's name alone") re-introduces exactly the false positive that the previous fix's docstring called out — the sentence it deleted, "a bare file name is in every test that writes one of its own." Because the fallback matches on the bare file name with no directory scoping, any test whose source mentions that name is selected, even when it cannot read the changed file. Concrete input: the repo contains `tests/fixtures/sets/corpus.jsonl`, a reader `tests/test_run_time_path.py` with `C = FIXTURES / "corpus.jsonl"`, and an unrelated `tests/test_writes_own.py` containing `(tmp_path / "corpus.jsonl").write_text("x")`. When `tests/fixtures/sets/corpus.jsonl` changes, no test spells `sets/corpus.jsonl` or `sets` (rule 1 and rule 2 miss), so the third rule matches `corpus.jsonl` and selects BOTH tests, including the writer that only creates its own `tmp_path/corpus.jsonl` and can never read the changed fixture. The same happens with two same-named data files in sibling directories: with `tests/alpha/data.json` changed and only `tests/test_beta.py` containing `P = "beta/data.json"`, rule 1 looks for `alpha/data.json`, rule 2 for the nearest dir `alpha`, both miss, and rule 3's bare `data.json` matches the beta reader, selecting a test that reads a different file. The change also deletes the `tests/other/COPYING` case from `test_a_farther_directory_alone_is_not_evidence`, i.e. the very assertion that previously pinned down "a bare file name is not evidence" — so nothing in the suite now guards this regression.

chunk_findings.detail: The rung list builds a "directory alone" rung for *every* directory in `dirs`, not just the nearest one, contradicting the stated rule ("…; failing that, the nearest such directory; failing that, the file's name; stop at the first rung that hits") and the function's own docstring ("the nearest such directory alone"). Concretely, with tests living only under `tests/`, a change to `tests/fixtures/data/report.json` makes `_dirs_below_tests` return `["data", "fixtures"]`. If no test spells `data` but many tests spell `fixtures` (for their own, unrelated fixture files), rung 2 skips past the nearest directory, matches `fixtures`, and selects every such test — tests that never name `report.json` or its directory `data` and therefore cannot read the changed file. And because selection stops at the first hitting rung, a test that *does* read the file by its exact name (the intended last-resort name rung) is never reached. Under the stated rule the nearest directory failing should fall through to the file's name, not to a farther, generic ancestor directory.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/testselect.py:_data_readers (the `rungs = ...` line)

chunk_findings.detail: The right-hand boundary is `(?![\w-])`, which omits `.`, while the left-hand boundary is `(?<![\w.-])`, which includes it. The helper therefore still matches a name as a prefix of a longer dotted name, contradicting its documented contract ("not inside a longer name"): `_names("tmp_path / 'LICENSE.txt'", "LICENSE")` returns True, as does `_names('"fixtures.json"', "fixtures")`. Given a changed data file `tests/fixtures/x.json` (whose nearest directory rung is `fixtures`), a test that only writes its own `fixtures.json` is selected as a reader of `x.json` even though it cannot read it. Excluding `.` on the right, as on the left, would remove these false positives.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own fixture states the invariant that a bare file name is not evidence a test reads that file — `tests/test_licence_writer.py` is described as "writes a COPYING of its own: the bare name is not evidence it reads this one". But the rule it is testing keeps a third rung, "failing that, the file's name", which does exactly what the comment says is invalid. The added test only observes `test_licence_writer` being skipped because `test_conformance` (which does read a COPYING) hits rung 1 first, so "stop at the first rung" masks the bug; the bare-name rung is never actually exercised. Concretely, give the rule a changed file whose directory nothing spells: add/modify `tests/other/COPYING` (no test source mentions `other`). Rung 1 fails (no source spells `COPYING` with `other`), rung 2 fails (nearest directory `other` is named by no test), so rung 3 matches `tests/test_licence_writer.py` on the bare string `"COPYING"` and selects it — a test that only writes its own COPYING and cannot read `tests/other/COPYING`. So the new rule still selects a test that cannot read the changed file, the failure mode the change's rationale claims to have eliminated.

chunk_findings.detail: The "failing that, the file's NEAREST directory alone" rung is built from the first element of `dirs`, but `dirs` holds the directories between the test root and the file in path order (outermost first), so `dirs[0]` is the *farthest* directory, not the nearest. For a changed file `tests/fixtures/guard_baselines/case.json` with tests under `tests/`, `dirs == ["fixtures", "guard_baselines"]`, so the second rung tests for the word `fixtures`. Consequence: (a) the test that actually reads the file and spells only its immediate directory (`guard_baselines`) is never matched, because it does not spell the generic `fixtures` — e.g. `os.path.join(BASE, "guard_baselines", name)` with `BASE` defined as `"fixtures"` elsewhere selects nothing, whereas `dirs[-1]` would match; and (b) conversely every test that merely names `fixtures` (i.e. reads any fixture at all) is selected as a reader of `case.json`, which is exactly the over-broad match the new docstring says the nearest-directory rung exists to avoid ("a farther directory (`fixtures`) is in every test that reads any fixture at all"). The code therefore contradicts both its own docstring ("NEAREST") and the retained comment ("most specific first"); the rung must use the deepest directory (`dirs[-1]`), not `dirs[0]`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new last-resort "file's name alone" tier is a purely textual match, so it cannot tell a test that builds the *right* directory from a constant apart from a test that mentions the same basename in an unrelated context. Concrete input: change `tests/fixtures/sets/corpus.jsonl`, and add a test file `tests/test_other_corpus.py` whose source is `C = FIXTURES / "other" / "corpus.jsonl"` (it reads `tests/fixtures/other/corpus.jsonl`, a different file). The file's own directories below `tests` are `fixtures/sets` and `sets`, and the test spells neither, nor does it spell the nearest directory `sets`; so the selection falls through to the name-alone tier and returns `{"tests/test_other_corpus.py": "names data file tests/fixtures/sets/corpus.jsonl"}` even though that test never opens the changed file. The same holds for a test that *writes* its own file, e.g. `(tmp_path / "corpus.jsonl").write_text(...)` — the old docstring even called this out ("a bare file name is in every test that writes one of its own"), and the new docstring's claim that the picked test "still reads the file" is not something the name-only rule can establish. This is a false positive in exactly the direction the task asks about: a test is selected that cannot read the changed file.

Given a changed data file `tests/fixtures/x.json` (whose nearest directory rung is `fixtures`), a test that only writes its own `fixtures.json` is selected as a reader of `x.json` even though it cannot read it. Excluding `.` on the right, as on the left, would remove these false positives.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own fixture states the invariant that a bare file name is not evidence a test reads that file — `tests/test_licence_writer.py` is described as "writes a COPYING of its own: the bare name is not evidence it reads this one". But the rule it is testing keeps a third rung, "failing that, the file's name", which does exactly what the comment says is invalid. The added test only observes `test_licence_writer` being skipped because `test_conformance` (which does read a COPYING) hits rung 1 first, so "stop at the first rung" masks the bug; the bare-name rung is never actually exercised. Concretely, give the rule a changed file whose directory nothing spells: add/modify `tests/other/COPYING` (no test source mentions `other`). Rung 1 fails (no source spells `COPYING` with `other`), rung 2 fails (nearest directory `other` is named by no test), so rung 3 matches `tests/test_licence_writer.py` on the bare string `"COPYING"` and selects it — a test that only writes its own COPYING and cannot read `tests/other/COPYING`. So the new rule still selects a test that cannot read the changed file, the failure mode the change's rationale claims to have eliminated.

chunk_findings.detail: The "failing that, the file's NEAREST directory alone" rung is built from the first element of `dirs`, but `dirs` holds the directories between the test root and the file in path order (outermost first), so `dirs[0]` is the *farthest* directory, not the nearest. For a changed file `tests/fixtures/guard_baselines/case.json` with tests under `tests/`, `dirs == ["fixtures", "guard_baselines"]`, so the second rung tests for the word `fixtures`. Consequence: (a) the test that actually reads the file and spells only its immediate directory (`guard_baselines`) is never matched, because it does not spell the generic `fixtures` — e.g. `os.path.join(BASE, "guard_baselines", name)` with `BASE` defined as `"fixtures"` elsewhere selects nothing, whereas `dirs[-1]` would match; and (b) conversely every test that merely names `fixtures` (i.e. reads any fixture at all) is selected as a reader of `case.json`, which is exactly the over-broad match the new docstring says the nearest-directory rung exists to avoid ("a farther directory (`fixtures`) is in every test that reads any fixture at all"). The code therefore contradicts both its own docstring ("NEAREST") and the retained comment ("most specific first"); the rung must use the deepest directory (`dirs[-1]`), not `dirs[0]`.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/services/testselect.py` `_data_readers` (the `rungs =` line, ~new line 245)

chunk_findings.detail: The new last-resort "file's name alone" tier is a purely textual match, so it cannot tell a test that builds the *right* directory from a constant apart from a test that mentions the same basename in an unrelated context. Concrete input: change `tests/fixtures/sets/corpus.jsonl`, and add a test file `tests/test_other_corpus.py` whose source is `C = FIXTURES / "other" / "corpus.jsonl"` (it reads `tests/fixtures/other/corpus.jsonl`, a different file). The file's own directories below `tests` are `fixtures/sets` and `sets`, and the test spells neither, nor does it spell the nearest directory `sets`; so the selection falls through to the name-alone tier and returns `{"tests/test_other_corpus.py": "names data file tests/fixtures/sets/corpus.jsonl"}` even though that test never opens the changed file. The same holds for a test that *writes* its own file, e.g. `(tmp_path / "corpus.jsonl").write_text(...)` — the old docstring even called this out ("a bare file name is in every test that writes one of its own"), and the new docstring's claim that the picked test "still reads the file" is not something the name-only rule can establish. This is a false positive in exactly the direction the task asks about: a test is selected that cannot read the changed file.

chunk_findings.detail:
The fallback that catches a reader with a run‑time‑built part is gated on the specific rung being empty (`if not hit:`), so any single test that spells the file's name together with one of its directories suppresses the fallback for the whole file and hides every reader whose only spelled-out part is the name (or the nearest directory). The module docstring names exactly such readers (`FIXTURES / "corpus.jsonl"`, `BASELINES / f"{kind}.toml"`) as what the union exists to catch; the code only catches them when no other test spells name+directory.

Demonstration: changed file `tests/fixtures/mcp-schema/LICENSE`. `tests/test_precise.py` contains the literal `"fixtures/mcp-schema/LICENSE"`; `tests/test_constant.py` does `SCHEMA / "LICENSE"` where `SCHEMA` comes from a shared constant, so it spells `LICENSE` but no directory that appears in `dirs`. The first rung returns `[test_precise]` (non‑empty), `if not hit` is false, and `test_constant` — a genuine reader of the changed file — is never added to `out`, so a change to `LICENSE` runs only `test_precise` and the breakage `test_constant` would show is deferred to the gate. The same holds for the `BASELINES / f"{kind}.toml"` shape: once any test spells `guard_baselines/alpha.toml`, the reader that only names `guard_baselines` is dropped before the `names(t, dirs[0])` branch can be evaluated.

chunk_findings.detail: The old expression `repo_relative(repo, f, as_given=True) or str(f)` explicitly guarded against the case where the helper yields no usable path, substituting the file's own path. The new expression `repo_rel(repo, f, as_given=True, strict=False)` drops that fallback. `strict` only governs whether the outside-the-repo case raises or yields no result; with `strict=False` the function has nothing repo-relative to return for a path that is not under `repo` (e.g. a file given as `/tmp/notes.md` while `repo` is `/r`), so `rel` is `None`/empty instead of the path. Given such a file in `files`, the loop then stores/renders `rel` as the source identifier (added to `named`, used as the location label for any needle hit), producing `None` labels instead of the old `str(f)`, and any later string use of `rel` (formatting, `split`, path joining) raises `AttributeError`/`TypeError`. To preserve the old behavior the call needs the same `or str(f)` fallback the deleted code had.

chunk_findings.detail: The old expression `repo_relative(repo, f, as_given=True) or str(f)` is a two-part idiom: `repo_relative` returns a repo-relative string when it can, and `None` when the path is not under `repo`, at which point `or str(f)` substituted the caller's path. `repo_rel` is that same routine with a `strict` flag added: `strict=True` is the raising mode, and `strict=False` is the non-raising mode that returns `None` for an out-of-repo path — this is exactly why the old call site needed the `or str(f)` guard, and the merged function keeps that non-strict contract rather than inventing a `str(f)` fallback. Dropping the guard therefore changes behavior for any input not under `repo`: pass `f = /tmp/notes.md` (or a doc from a sibling checkout) and `rel` becomes `None` instead of `"/tmp/notes.md"`. The loop around this line builds `named: set[str]` and formats those relative paths as the pin locations; a `None` member makes later `sorted(named)`/`"\n".join(named)` raise `TypeError` (or renders the literal "None"), so a single out-of-repo file aborts the whole pin pass — precisely the failure mode the comment above this loop says must not happen ("One bad file must not hide…"). Restore `or str(f)` unless `repo_rel(..., strict=False)` is explicitly documented to return the path as given.

chunk_findings.detail: The sentinel is `"?! "`, i.e. it begins with `?`, which is precisely the `git status --porcelain` column value for an untracked entry, and `!` is a legal porcelain column value too (ignored). The comment claims `Not a porcelain status code, so it cannot be mistaken for a file`, but that is not what makes a line safe: what matters is how consumers *classify* porcelain lines. Any caller that tolerates untracked entries (which this file's own `dirty` docstring says is exactly the situation — `merge` used to refuse because untracked build directories / `.ddflow/` were counted as dirty, so untracked-tolerant handling exists) and keys on the first status character will discard the marker. For example, with a caller of the shape `changes = [ln for ln in dirty(wt) if not ln.startswith("?")]` (or `all(ln[0] == "?" for ln in dirty(wt))`), an unreadable tree now yields `[]` / `True`, i.e. “clean”, which is the very `B028b11b4cb` failure this change is meant to remove. Only `remove` is protected because it is the single call site that explicitly calls `unreadable()`; every other consumer of `dirty`/`W.dirty` gets a line that is indistinguishable from an untracked status by first-character inspection. A marker built from characters that can never appear in a porcelain status (so that no untracked/ignored/dirty classifier can match it) is required for the “never mistaken for a file/clean” property the comment asserts.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/worktree.py:370 (`UNREADABLE = "?! "`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_measure` signals "unknown" by returning a *stripped* reason string and signals "measured fine" by returning `""`. When `W.dirty` reports an unreadable tree whose sentinel carries no message — i.e. `W.dirty(wt) == [W.UNREADABLE]` (a bare sentinel, which is exactly what a "git failed" branch that has no stderr/detail would produce, and the `dirty[0][len(W.UNREADABLE):]` slice is written to tolerate precisely this shape) — the expression `dirty[0][len(W.UNREADABLE):]` evaluates to `""`. `_measure` then returns `""`, the caller reads it as "could be measured", `t.dirty_files` is never assigned (the early `return` skipped line `t.dirty_files = len(dirty)`), and `_classify` falls through the `unknown` branch to `elif t.dirty_files:` (0/None, falsy) and `else: t.kind = "merged" if t.item else "orphan"; t.action = "remove"`. The result is that an unreadable worktree — the exact case this change exists to protect — is classified as fully merged and marked for automatic removal, so the bug is not fixed for sentinels without a message. Either `W.dirty` must guarantee a non-empty reason after the prefix, or the function should return a separate boolean/sentinel (e.g. return `None` on success, or check `W.unreadable(dirty)` truthiness in `_classify`) instead of overloading `""`.

chunk_findings.detail: The only new assertion is a tautology and guards none of the behaviour the change claims to fix. `slow` is defined on the line above as `S.TTL_S / 2 + 0.5`, so `2 * slow` is identically `S.TTL_S + 1`, which is always `> S.TTL_S` for any `TTL_S`. It therefore cannot fail — including on the unfixed configuration. Concretely: if you revert `LOADED_TTL_S`/`CI_LATENCY_S` (or someone later shrinks the lease back to 8s), `slow = 4.5`, `2*slow = 9 > 8` still passes, so the regression that motivated the change (headroom smaller than the machine's `show`+`claim` cost) is *not* detected by this assertion. The stated requirement "run this test under a longer TTL … with a test that the margin holds" is not implemented: the invariant that actually matters is `S.TTL_S - (slow + CI_LATENCY_S) > CI_LATENCY_S` (i.e. the remaining lease covers the measured 3.6–4.8 s real cost), and no such check exists. The added assertion restates the scenario shape it already had (`two injections outlive the lease`) rather than the margin, so it provides false assurance.

chunk_findings.detail: The added "regression test" never exercises the code under review. It calls `_cost(lambda: time.sleep(2.5))`, whose result depends only on the CPython standard library's `time.process_time` semantics; `check_docs`, `perf_counter`, and the budget logic are not touched. Concretely, apply this new test (plus the `_cost` helper) to the *unfixed* tree — i.e. keep `test_runtime_on_this_repositorys_readme` measuring with `time.perf_counter` — and the guard test still passes, so it does not fail on the unfixed code and does not reproduce B4d5ffa0b90. Likewise, if someone later reverts the main test to `time.perf_counter` while leaving `_cost` and this test in place, the guard still passes, so it provides no protection against regression of the actual fix. This contradicts the stated intent ("Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"): the only reason this test fails on a pre-change checkout is the `NameError` from the missing `_cost` symbol, not any timing behaviour, so it cannot discriminate fixed from unfixed code.

chunk_findings.detail: The newly added guard cannot fail, so it does not verify the margin the docstring claims to establish. Immediately after the monkeypatch, `slow` is defined as `S.TTL_S / 2 + 0.5`, so `2 * slow == S.TTL_S + 1`, which is `> S.TTL_S` identically for every value of the (already patched) `S.TTL_S`. Concretely, if a future edit (or an accidental revert) sets `LOADED_TTL_S` back to `8`, the assertion still passes (`2 * 4.5 = 9 > 8`), even though the injected sleep `slow + CI_LATENCY_S = 9.3s` then exceeds the lease and one check no longer fits — i.e. exactly the Bb070dd642d failure mode the test exists to detect. Worse, the assertion validates `slow` while the code actually sleeps `slow + CI_LATENCY_S`, so it is not even checking the duration that determines whether one check fits. To actually test "one alone fits, two together do not" you would need something like `slow + CI_LATENCY_S + tolerance < S.TTL_S` and `2 * (slow + CI_LATENCY_S) > S.TTL_S`.

chunk_findings.detail: The added "regression" test never touches `check_docs` or the budget assertion; it only asserts that `time.process_time()` does not advance across `time.sleep(2.5)`, which is a property of the stdlib, not of the code under change. Concretely: if you write the test first by adding only `_cost` + this test and leave `test_runtime_on_this_repositorys_readme` measuring with `time.perf_counter()` (i.e. the bug still present), this test is still green — it fails only when the `_cost` helper is absent (NameError at collection), never because the runtime budget counted wall time. So it does not reproduce B4d5ffa0b90 and provides no protection against a future regression reverting the runtime test to a wall clock, while unconditionally adding 2.5 s of wall time (more under the very load it describes) to every run of the suite.

Moreover, the test does not exercise the actual behavioral delta of this diff at all: the only thing `_cpu()` adds over `process_time()` is `children_user + children_system` (the CPU of the `git ls-files` subprocess). A test whose only manipulation is a no-CPU `sleep` passes even if `_cpu()` omitted the `children_*` terms, so it cannot detect a regression in the very accounting this change introduces. chunk_findings.detail: The change binds this new test as the regression test for B4d5ffa0b90, whose whole point is that the budget must be paid in CPU time rather than wall time. But the test cannot distinguish the two time sources. Its only observable is `spent > 0.1` for a CPU-bound subprocess (`sum(range(2 * 10**7))`). A CPU-bound child has wall time >= CPU time >= ~0.3 s on any current machine, so `spent` exceeds 0.1 s whether `_cost`/`_cpu` return `perf_counter()` wall time or `os.times()` CPU time. Concretely: on the unfixed implementation that measured `time.perf_counter()`, `spent` for the burn child is ~0.3–1 s, the assertion passes, and the test goes green — so it would not have failed on the pre-fix code and does not guard the regression. The test only exercises one half of the intended property (that a waited-for child is charged at all); a sibling child that merely `time.sleep()`s (wall > 0.1 s, CPU ~0) would be needed to show that wall time is *not* charged. As written, `ddflow complete fix-B4d5ffa0b90 --regression-test tests/test_docscheck_core.py::test_the_budget_charges_the_cpu_of_a_child_it_waited_for` records a regression test that cannot regress the bug it names (the existing descheduled test that sleeps `RUNTIME_BUDGET_S + 0.1` is the one that actually catches wall-clock measurement).

chunk_findings.detail: `suite_gates` selects "test suite" gates with a two-letter substring, `"ui"`, against `g.id`. Substring matching is not token matching, so ordinary build/lint gate names are swept in. For example, the string `"ui"` occurs inside `"build"` (b-**ui**-ld), `"quick_check"` (q-**ui**-ck...), and `"require"` (req-**ui**-re). Given a project whose config defines a normal command gate with id `build`, `suite_gates` returns `["build"]` because `"ui" in "build"` is `True`, and `render_command` feeds that list into the rendered `all-tests` command as `test_gates`. The rendered output then instructs the agent that `build` is one of the extra test suites to run, which is wrong — a gate that merely contains the letters "ui" is not a UI/E2E/smoke/integration suite. The same false positive appears for any gate whose id happens to contain those two letters (e.g. `quick_*`, `require_*`, `fluid`), so the list the command advertises does not correspond to the suites that actually exist. A word-boundary/tokenized match (or a longer, unambiguous needle) is required for the `ui` case.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `arg` property is declared as `"array"`, but the conversion `[str(x) for x in (a.get("arg") or [])]` will silently iterate a string character-by-character if any caller (model-facing tool arguments are not reliably schema-validated, and the description literally tells the caller these are "KEY=VALUE arguments") passes a single string rather than a list. Concrete input: `{"action": "get", "name": "deploy", "arg": "env=prod"}`. `a.get("arg")` is the truthy string `"env=prod"`, so the comprehension yields `['e','n','v','=','p','r','o','d']` instead of `['env=prod']`. `prompts()` then receives eight single-character tokens, so the macro's parameter parser never sees the `env` key paired with `prod` and reports a missing/invalid parameter even though the caller supplied it. The fix must coerce a bare string to a one-element list (e.g. `[arg] if isinstance(arg, str) else [str(x) for x in arg]`) before forwarding; otherwise the exact "parameter check" this change is meant to route through the shared render path fails for a plausible caller input.

chunk_findings.detail: The new lambda coerces the argument with `arg=[str(x) for x in (a.get("arg") or [])]`. For a list this is fine, but if `arg` is supplied as a single scalar (which is very common when a model invokes a tool and only one KEY=VALUE is needed), the `or []` guard does not catch it and the comprehension iterates the string character by character. Demonstrated input: `{"action": "get", "name": "my_macro", "arg": "x=1"}` produces `["x", "=", "1"]` instead of `["x=1"]`, so `prompts()` receives three malformed argument fragments. The macro's required-parameter binding then either fails the au to-check this fix is meant to enforce, or binds a garbage key (`"x"`/`"="`/`"1"`) instead of `x=1`, i.e. the exact parameter-check path this change is supposed to make MCP and CLI share misbehaves for scalar input. Accepting either a string or a list (e.g. wrap non-list values) would remove the failure mode.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten `render_command` sources macros through `_macro_report(repo)[0]`, i.e. it takes only index 0 of the report and discards everything else. Its newly-added docstring, however, promises that it raises `TemplateError` "for ... a macro config that could not be read (with the reason, as MCP says it)". Nothing in the shown code can produce that: the only macro-config access is `_macro_report(repo)[0]`, and the only `TemplateError` raised on the macro path is the `macro is None` branch, whose message is `"unknown prompt {name!r}. Known: ..."`. So on a repo whose `[[macro]]` config fails to load/parse, the two branches of `_macro_report`'s report are handled wrongly: (a) if the report carries the read failure in its second element, that element is dropped, and CLI `ddflow prompts get X` answers "unknown prompt 'X'. Known: …" while MCP `prompts/get` answers with the actual read reason; (b) if `_macro_report` raises `macros.MacroError` instead, that call sits *outside* the `try` (which only wraps `M.render`), and the `except P.TemplateError` in `api/setup.py::_prompts_get` can no longer catch it because this same diff removed the `MacroError` arm from that except tuple — so the CLI raises an uncaught exception rather than returning a failed `Outcome`. Either way the CLI and MCP diverge on exactly the input the change was meant to unify (a macro config that cannot be read), and the documented contract is not implemented.

chunk_findings.detail: The new docstring promises that `render_command` "Raises `TemplateError` for ... a macro config that could not be read (with the reason, as MCP says it)", and the diff correspondingly narrows the caller to `except P.TemplateError` / deletes `from ..services.macros import MacroError` in `_prompts_get` (ddflow/api/setup.py). But the read of the macro config is done by `macro = _macro_report(repo)[0].get(name)`, which sits *outside* the only new `try/except M.MacroError` block; that block wraps only `M.render(macro, ...)`. So the config-read failure is never converted: if `_macro_report` signals an unreadable macro config by raising `macros.MacroError` (which is the only way the promised "reason" can reach the caller, since the code discards `_macro_report`'s report element and never formats a reason into its own `TemplateError` message), that `MacroError` escapes `render_command`, and because `_prompts_get` no longer catches `MacroError`, `ddflow prompts get <macro>` dies with an unhandled `MacroError` traceback instead of the `TemplateError` the docstring specifies. If instead `_macro_report` returns the reason as a report, then the reason is silently dropped and a broken macro is reported as `unknown prompt 'x'` — again contradicting the documented behavior. Reproduction: put a malformed `[[macro]]` entry in the repo's config (so the macro set cannot be read), then run `ddflow prompts get <name>`; the intended outcome is a `TemplateError` carrying the read failure, the actual outcome is either an uncaught `MacroError` or an "unknown prompt" message with no reason. Widen the try to cover `_macro_report(repo)` (or otherwise surface its report) before claiming `TemplateError` for this case.

chunk_findings.detail: `arg=list(getattr(a, "arg", None) or [])` was changed to `arg=getattr(a, "arg", None)`, which drops the `None -> []` coercion. The sibling surface that now feeds the same renderer keeps exactly that coercion: `maintenance.py` still does `list(a.get("arg") or [])` for the non-string branch, and it additionally wraps a bare string. So the shared code path (`api.prompts` / the new `render_command`, which must at minimum iterate `arg` to split each `KEY=VALUE`) receives a list from the tool surface but `None` from the CLI surface. Concretely: run this command omitting `--arg` (e.g. a macro without required params, or the `show`/`get` probe cases the bug is about). `a.arg` is absent/None, `arg=None` is forwarded, and the KEY=VALUE parser raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable` rather than taking the empty-argument path that the old `or []` guaranteed. Either the `or []` (matching maintenance.py) should be restored, or the renderer has to accept `None`; the current combination is inconsistent between the two callers of the supposedly unified function.

chunk_findings.detail: `suite_gates` selects "test suite" gates with a two-letter substring, `"ui"`, against `g.id`. Substring matching is not token matching, so ordinary build/lint gate names are swept in. For example, the string `"ui"` occurs inside `"build"` (b-**ui**-ld), `"quick_check"` (q-**ui**-ck...), and `"require"` (req-**ui**-re). Given a project whose config defines a normal command gate with id `build`, `suite_gates` returns `["build"]` because `"ui" in "build"` is `True`, and `render_command` feeds that list into the rendered `all-tests` command as `test_gates`. The rendered output then instructs the agent that `build` is one of the extra test suites to run, which is wrong — a gate that merely contains the letters "ui" is not a UI/E2E/smoke/integration suite. The same false positive appears for any gate whose id happens to contain those two letters (e.g. `quick_*`, `require_*`, `fluid`), so the list the command advertises does not correspond to the suites that actually exist. A word-boundary/tokenized match (or a longer, unambiguous needle) is required for the `ui` case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/prompts.py:suite_gates (the `any(w in g.id ...)` filter)

chunk_findings.detail: The new `arg` property is declared as `"array"`, but the conversion `[str(x) for x in (a.get("arg") or [])]` will silently iterate a string character-by-character if any caller (model-facing tool arguments are not reliably schema-validated, and the description literally tells the caller these are "KEY=VALUE arguments") passes a single string rather than a list. Concrete input: `{"action": "get", "name": "deploy", "arg": "env=prod"}`. `a.get("arg")` is the truthy string `"env=prod"`, so the comprehension yields `['e','n','v','=','p','r','o','d']` instead of `['env=prod']`. `prompts()` then receives eight single-character tokens, so the macro's parameter parser never sees the `env` key paired with `prod` and reports a missing/invalid parameter even though the caller supplied it. The fix must coerce a bare string to a one-element list (e.g. `[arg] if isinstance(arg, str) else [str(x) for x in arg]`) before forwarding; otherwise the exact "parameter check" this change is meant to route through the shared render path fails for a plausible caller input.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten `render_command` sources macros through `_macro_report(repo)[0]`, i.e. it takes only index 0 of the report and discards everything else. Its newly-added docstring, however, promises that it raises `TemplateError` "for ... a macro config that could not be read (with the reason, as MCP says it)". Nothing in the shown code can produce that: the only macro-config access is `_macro_report(repo)[0]`, and the only `TemplateError` raised on the macro path is the `macro is None` branch, whose message is `"unknown prompt {name!r}. Known: ..."`. So on a repo whose `[[macro]]` config fails to load/parse, the two branches of `_macro_report`'s report are handled wrongly: (a) if the report carries the read failure in its second element, that element is dropped, and CLI `ddflow prompts get X` answers "unknown prompt 'X'. Known: …" while MCP `prompts/get` answers with the actual read reason; (b) if `_macro_report` raises `macros.MacroError` instead, that call sits *outside* the `try` (which only wraps `M.render`), and the `except P.TemplateError` in `api/setup.py::_prompts_get` can no longer catch it because this same diff removed the `MacroError` arm from that except tuple — so the CLI raises an uncaught exception rather than returning a failed `Outcome`. Either way the CLI and MCP diverge on exactly the input the change was meant to unify (a macro config that cannot be read), and the documented contract is not implemented.

chunk_findings.detail: The comment justifies the coercion with "a schema-violating MCP client may send a number", but `map(str, pairs)` only handles a *container of* non-strings; the container itself must be iterable. If a schema-violating client sends a scalar number for `arg` (the case the comment names), e.g. `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"ddflow_prompts","arguments":{"action":"get","name":"implement","arg":5}}}`, then `map(str, 5)` raises `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable` instead of returning the `argument ...: expected KEY=VALUE` failure — the same -32603 crash this hunk is meant to prevent. The regression test only exercises the list form (`"arg": [1]`), so it does not cover the single-number input the comment claims to handle.

The predicate `any(w in g.id for w in ("test", "e2e", "smoke", "integration", "ui"))` is True for e.g. `g.id == "build"` (`b-u-i-l-d`) or `"require"` (`r-e-q-u-i-r-e`), so for a project that configures a non-test command gate named `build`, `suite_gates(repo)` returns `["build"]` and the `test_gates` value injected into the `all-tests` command render (line ~563, `"test_gates": suite_gates(repo)`) names a non-test gate as a suite. chunk_findings.detail: The new lambda coerces the argument with `arg=[str(x) for x in (a.get("arg") or [])]`. For a list this is fine, but if `arg` is supplied as a single scalar (which is very common when a model invokes a tool and only one KEY=VALUE is needed), the `or []` guard does not catch it and the comprehension iterates the string character by character. Demonstrated input: `{"action": "get", "name": "my_macro", "arg": "x=1"}` produces `["x", "=", "1"]` instead of `["x=1"]`, so `prompts()` receives three malformed argument fragments. The macro's required-parameter binding then either fails the au to-check this fix is meant to enforce, or binds a garbage key (`"x"`/`"="`/`"1"`) instead of `x=1`, i.e. the exact parameter-check path this change is supposed to make MCP and CLI share misbehaves for scalar input. Accepting either a string or a list (e.g. wrap non-list values) would remove the failure mode.

chunk_findings.detail: The new docstring promises that `render_command` "Raises `TemplateError` for ... a macro config that could not be read (with the reason, as MCP says it)", and the diff correspondingly narrows the caller to `except P.TemplateError` / deletes `from ..services.macros import MacroError` in `_prompts_get` (ddflow/api/setup.py). But the read of the macro config is done by `macro = _macro_report(repo)[0].get(name)`, which sits *outside* the only new `try/except M.MacroError` block; that block wraps only `M.render(macro, ...)`. So the config-read failure is never converted: if `_macro_report` signals an unreadable macro config by raising `macros.MacroError` (which is the only way the promised "reason" can reach the caller, since the code discards `_macro_report`'s report element and never formats a reason into its own `TemplateError` message), that `MacroError` escapes `render_command`, and because `_prompts_get` no longer catches `MacroError`, `ddflow prompts get <macro>` dies with an unhandled `MacroError` traceback instead of the `TemplateError` the docstring specifies. If instead `_macro_report` returns the reason as a report, then the reason is silently dropped and a broken macro is reported as `unknown prompt 'x'` — again contradicting the documented behavior. Reproduction: put a malformed `[[macro]]` entry in the repo's config (so the macro set cannot be read), then run `ddflow prompts get <name>`; the intended outcome is a `TemplateError` carrying the read failure, the actual outcome is either an uncaught `MacroError` or an "unknown prompt" message with no reason. Widen the try to cover `_macro_report(repo)` (or otherwise surface its report) before claiming `TemplateError` for this case.

chunk_findings.detail: `arg=list(getattr(a, "arg", None) or [])` was changed to `arg=getattr(a, "arg", None)`, which drops the `None -> []` coercion. The sibling surface that now feeds the same renderer keeps exactly that coercion: `maintenance.py` still does `list(a.get("arg") or [])` for the non-string branch, and it additionally wraps a bare string. So the shared code path (`api.prompts` / the new `render_command`, which must at minimum iterate `arg` to split each `KEY=VALUE`) receives a list from the tool surface but `None` from the CLI surface. Concretely: run this command omitting `--arg` (e.g. a macro without required params, or the `show`/`get` probe cases the bug is about). `a.arg` is absent/None, `arg=None` is forwarded, and the KEY=VALUE parser raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable` rather than taking the empty-argument path that the old `or []` guaranteed. Either the `or []` (matching maintenance.py) should be restored, or the renderer has to accept `None`; the current combination is inconsistent between the two callers of the supposedly unified function.

chunk_findings.detail: `map(str, pairs)` coerces rather than rejects non-string arguments, so the guard is incomplete. For input `{"action":"get","name":"implement","arg":[["mode=fast"]]}`, `str([["mode=fast"]])` is `"[['mode=fast']]"`, which contains `=`; `partition("=")` yields key `"[['mode"` and value `"fast']]"`, and because `key.strip()` is truthy this passes the `not eq or not key.strip()` check and is accepted into `args` instead of being refused. The test's premise ("a non-string tool argument is refused") therefore holds only for scalars like `1`; nested containers whose repr contains `=` are silently misparsed.

chunk_findings.detail: The snapshot compare is asymmetric: `before` is built from every file under `repo/.ddflow`, but `after` is filtered to drop `.lock`/`.gitignore` while `before` is not. The code's own comment ("The local layer's own .gitignore and the write lock are not config") acknowledges that `repo/.ddflow/.gitignore` is part of the local layer. When the fixture/harness has already materialised the local layer (so `repo/.ddflow/.gitignore` exists before the call), `before` contains the `.gitignore` entry and `after` has it filtered out, so `after == before` is False and the test fails with "a refused block still changed a config file" even though production code correctly refused the block and wrote nothing. Concretely: any run where `repo/.ddflow/.gitignore` pre-exists makes this regression test fail on the *fixed* code, so it cannot validate the fix (and would wrongly be read as "fix still writes"). The same applies to any pre-existing `*.lock` in the local layer. The filter needs to be applied to `before` as well (or both snapshots should be captured the same way).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_append_block_schema.py:26-38 (`test_a_reviewer_block_with_an_unknown_field_is_refused_and_nothing_is_written`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `before` snapshot (lines 22-26) is taken with `{p: p.read_bytes() for p in (repo / ".ddflow").rglob("*") if p.is_file()}` — i.e. *all* files — but the `after` snapshot is then filtered with `after = {p: b for p, b in after.items() if not p.name.endswith((".lock", ".gitignore"))}`. The two sides that are compared are therefore not computed the same way. If the `repo` fixture (or an earlier configuration write, or a session/module-scoped `repo` reused by the second parametrized run) leaves a `.ddflow/.gitignore` or a `*.lock` file in place before `append_block` is called, `before` will contain that entry while `after` will have dropped it, so `after == before` is False and the test fails even though the refused call wrote nothing. Given the test itself guards on `(repo / ".ddflow").exists()` — acknowledging the directory may already exist — and the comment says these files "are not config", the filter must be applied to `before` too, otherwise the regression test false-fails exactly in the environment it is meant to verify.

chunk_findings.detail:
The refactor moves the reviewer-schema check into `_check_reviewer_fields`, but adds a guard (`if isinstance(raw, dict)`) that the code it replaced did not have. chunk_findings.detail: The promotion nodes are built as `"promote_" + _node(g)`, while task-pipeline nodes use bare `_node(g)`. This mapping is not injective: any task gate whose sanitized id already equals `"promote_" + <sanitized promotion gate>` collides with the promotion node of the same name. Concretely, given `cfg.gates.task_pipeline == ["promote_test", "review"]` and a running promotion pipeline `["test"]`, the code emits `nodes = ["Claim", "promote_test", "review", "Complete", "promote_test", "Promoted"]`; mermaid treats repeated ids as one node, so the emitted flowchart becomes a cycle `Claim→promote_test→review→Complete→promote_test→Promoted` with `promote_test` having two incoming/outgoing edges, instead of the intended two distinct steps. The inline comment ("Prefixed: a gate in both pipelines is a different step in each") only holds for the same gate id appearing in both pipelines; it does not hold for distinct gate ids that already carry the `promote_` prefix, so the diagram silently misrepresents the flow for that configuration.

chunk_findings.detail: The new contract in `_diagram`'s docstring/comment is that "every step [gets] its own node" — but the collision-avoidance loop is only reachable inside `if promotion:` and only runs for the promotion entries. Task-gate node ids are still built with a bare `[_node(g) for g in pipeline]` and are never checked against what is already in `nodes`, so two task gates whose ids normalize to the same node collapse into one node (the second becomes a self-loop and the step disappears from the flow). Given `cfg.gates.task_pipeline = ["a.b", "a-b"]`, `_node` maps both to `"a_b"`, `nodes` becomes `["Claim", "a_b", "a_b", "Complete"]`, and the emitted Mermaid is `Claim --> a_b[a.b]` followed by `a_b --> a_b[a-b]` — a self-loop on a single node instead of two distinct steps. The same happens whenever a task gate normalizes to `Claim`/`Complete` (e.g. a gate id `Complete` yields `Complete --> Complete[Complete]`, merging the gate with the terminal sentinel). The promotion branch was hardened with `while node in nodes: node += "_"`, but the same normalization-collision is left unfixed for the task pipeline, so the stated "one node per step" guarantee is false for the very input the fix advertises it handles.

chunk_findings.detail: This regression test cannot fail for the bug it is named after. It calls `_diagram(["promote_test", "review"], ["test", "Promoted"])` and asserts the arrow targets are unique. The prior B726755d8f7 collision was two *steps that resolve to the same node id* (e.g. the same gate id appearing in both `task_pipeline` and `promotion_pipeline`, or two labels that sanitise to the same slug). Here the two step ids (`promote_test`, `review`) and the two labels (`test`, `Promoted`) are all distinct, so under any plausible pre-fix derivation of the node id — the raw step id, the raw/slugged label, the token before `_`, the token after `_` — the targets are already distinct and the assertion passes. I.e. the test would pass against the pre-fix code in 4cc8793b's parent, so a future regression that reinstates node merging (same gate id drawn once across two pipelines) will not be caught. To actually exercise the fix the test must supply two steps/labels that collide pre-fix, e.g. `_diagram(["unit_tests", "unit_tests"], [...])` or two labels whose slugs are identical.

chunk_findings.detail: The helper is called with `rerun=prior`, where `prior` is the middle value returned by `_announce_rerun(rerun, revs, item, gate, say)` on the line immediately above. `prior` is named for, and holds, the prior review record/evidence for this gate, and it is non-empty precisely when the item has been reviewed before — i.e. on exactly the re-reviews this change is supposed to fix. The first statement of the helper, `if kind != "full" or rerun or it is None: return context`, therefore short-circuits to the unmodified `context` on every ordinary full re-review. Concretely: take an item whose last review reported findings, run a normal (non `--delta-only`) re-review; `kind == "full"` but `prior` is truthy, so the function returns before ever reaching `_last_review(...).get("chunk_findings")`, and the prompt contains none of the "## Previous findings on this change, and the author's triage" block. The reviewer is back to seeing the diff without the prior findings/triage, which is the exact D-gate-economy 3 regression the change is meant to eliminate. Note the helper's own docstring lists only "a first review, a delta ... or a `--chunk` re-run (`rerun`)" as no-op cases — an ordinary full re-review is not among them — so the code contradicts its stated contract. The guard should key on the chunk/delta-only indicator (the `only` value / the raw rerun request), not on the mere existence of a prior review record; and if `_announce_rerun` has already replaced the gate's current record, `_last_review` will also no longer hold the previous findings, so the prior findings should come from `prior` itself rather than a re-read.
